source.title: Regularization-wise double descent: Why it occurs and how to eliminate it

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary sections are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error across training epochs in its own neural-network experiments, bearing directly on epoch-wise double descent. It also tests regularization-related refinements, but does not reproduce the model-size, sample-size, or other original sweeps.
record.gate_note: The model-size and sample-wise findings in the related-work discussion are attributed to other papers and are not results from this study. The paper's own regularization-strength sweeps are included only where they bear on V6. The dropout sweep reports a U-shaped curve, not a double-descent result relevant to these versions.
record.test_reason: The paper's own experiments measure test risk over training epochs or iterations for a 5-layer CNN and a two-layer network (V2). They also show that tuned weight decay removes the epoch-wise peak in the CNN (V6). Most of the paper studies a different axis, the risk as a function of the ℓ2 strength 1/λ, which no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ℓ2-regularized models, including standard deep networks with and without label noise, can show double descent in regularization strength. They explain it as superposed bias-variance tradeoffs of different features or network parts, removable by scaling regularization per part. They also stress that ℓ2 regularization and early stopping behave differently.
record.recipe_differences: The study focuses on risk across explicit regularization strength and layer/feature-specific regularization. Its epoch-wise experiments use particular CNN and two-layer settings; the text does not state that it reproduces the original study's full model-size or sample-size procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve changes with regularization setup: layer-specific scaling eliminates some regularization-wise curves; early stopping eliminates regularization-wise double descent in the CNN experiment; tuned weight decay eliminates epoch-wise double descent. The noiseless CIFAR-100 curve is described as subtler than the noisy-data curves, though dataset and model comparisons do not isolate noise as the cause.

fits_no_version.finding: Test risk as a function of inverse ℓ2 strength 1/λ is double-descent shaped: ridge regression in theory, a two-layer net, a 5-layer CNN and ResNet-18 on noisy CIFAR-10, and more subtly a CNN on clean CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization-wise double descent: test error first falls, rises, then falls again as explicit ℓ2 regularization is weakened.

fits_no_version.finding: The regularization-wise peak is a superposition of per-feature or per-layer bias-variance tradeoffs. Scaling λ per feature or per layer, or adding early stopping, removes it and lowers the best risk.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double-descent peaks along a regularization axis arise from misaligned bias-variance tradeoffs of model parts and vanish when part-wise regularization is aligned.

record.problems: Several neural-network outcomes are presented only in figures without tabulated values or reported uncertainty. The noisy CIFAR-10 and noiseless CIFAR-100 comparisons differ in dataset and do not isolate the effect of label noise. The reported regularization settings do not establish that globally optimal regularization always eliminates the curves.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were omitted. The cited model-size, sample-wise, and multiple-descent findings from other works were excluded because they are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: Only one CNN on noisy CIFAR-10 and one two-layer net on synthetic data. No range of architectures, noise levels or widths.
No capacity sweep past interpolation in any model class.
Does not vary label noise in a controlled way, does not test multiple peaks along epochs/size/samples, and does not test model- or sample-wise peak removal by optimal regularization.

missing.what: Dropout sweep on 5-layer CNN with noisy CIFAR-10 gives a U-shaped curve, not double descent (optimum p=0.4).

record.verdict_notes: Most rows concern a regularization-wise axis that no version names, so they were unlinked and moved to fits_no_version. The V2 evidence is a contrast figure that echoes Nakkiran et al. The paper's statement that more noise gives more pronounced curves is asserted, not tested under controlled conditions.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve across model sizes.
The epoch-wise tests cover particular CNN and two-layer network settings, not a broad range of deep-network architectures or datasets.
No sweep over training-sample count near an interpolation threshold.
The paper does not test risk across capacity in model classes as capacity passes an interpolation point.
It does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study tests elimination of some regularization-wise and epoch-wise curves through regularization choices, and reports curves in noisy and noiseless settings. It does not isolate whether label noise or variance causes the peak, test triple or multiple descent, or establish that globally optimal regularization always removes peaks.
No comparison against an effective parameter count or demonstration that the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve under that count.
